rationale: A wins because it keeps the founder closer to stories a reporter can actually defend, then forces the proof before outreach. “Whoop Calls Blood Pressure a ‘Wellness Estimate.’ That Word Choice Is Doing Legal Work.” is a sharp regulatory angle with the right caveat work attached. B has usable bones, but “Whoop's clinical features are also a pitch to its next investors” turns one valuation fact into a fundraising fairy tale. That is how a venture reporter deletes you before the coffee cools.
gaps_in_A: “Apple Watch Has Had It for Years” names Apple and implies timing not supplied in the update; it may be true, but the angle should stay generic until sourced.
“Apple Watch includes ECG with hardware, no subscription gate — confirm this” puts an unverified competitor-pricing claim inside the proof section. Good instinct, sloppy placement.

“That Word Choice Is Doing Legal Work” and “deliberate regulatory positioning move” slightly overstate intent. The facts support a wellness-vs-diagnostic line; they do not prove Whoop’s legal strategy.
“The wearable industry has spent years positioning cuffless blood pressure monitoring as the next frontier” needs sourcing. It is plausible context, not a supplied fact.
gaps_in_B: “Whoop's clinical features are also a pitch to its next investors” is the big miss. The update gives a private valuation, not fundraising, exit planning, or investor messaging.
“ahead of a future round or exit” is invented heat. B admits “none supplied here,” then pitches the story anyway.
“blood-pressure feature was designed to avoid that step” asserts intent the update does not establish. Non-diagnostic wellness framing is a fact; motive is not.
B wastes a slot on the speculative investor angle and misses the cleaner consumer story: “requires a one-time calibration with a cuff” is a real product-friction angle.
